title: Finish Like We’d Like to Start: The Return of These 6 Things
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a colleague's line -- 'we're just trying to finish the year like we'd like to start' -- Stuart applies his These 6 Things framework (heart-level motivation via the five key beliefs, knowledge-rich curricula, argument-rich curricula, reading, writing, and speaking/listening) to the final weeks of a pandemic-disrupted school year. He commits to a specific plan: running one belief-targeted intervention per student for each of the five key beliefs (credibility via moments of genuine connection, value via Chris Hulleman's Build Connections exercise, belonging via a values-affirmation exercise, effort via explicit study-skills instruction, and efficacy via a WOOP/GOOP goal-setting exercise), plus pursuing two extracurricular 'burning questions' to build knowledge beyond the mandated curriculum. He closes with three purposes for writing the piece: renewing his own motivation, offering readers a spark for their own final weeks, and cautioning that 'new isn't better by default' as schools plan pandemic-recovery changes.
points: The organizing principle -- 'finish the year like you'd like to start it' -- reframes the final weeks of school as a dress rehearsal for the fall rather than a countdown to survive.

Stuart operationalizes all five key beliefs into one concrete, time-boxed intervention apiece (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy), each with an explicit time estimate (1 to 30 minutes), making the abstract framework immediately actionable.

He distinguishes 'push' areas (one or two things you actively grow in each year) from 'maintain' areas (the rest, kept stable) as the discipline that keeps the six-things framework from becoming an unmanageable checklist.

He names a specific danger for post-disruption planning: 'there are two MASSIVE temptations... to chase after NEW because it seems like what you've been trying hasn't been working' and to reflexively resist new ideas -- both extremes he flags as untrustworthy defaults.
quotes: I was talking with my friend Dr. T a couple weeks back, and he said this line that had immediate resonance: “We're just trying to finish the year like we'd like to start.” That's just right.
The whole idea behind These 6 Things is that human beings can't become experts at everything. I'd like to, but I can't. I'm finite. So are you.

Instead, the idea is that as a professional you aim at mastering the use of these six elements. Your goal at all times is to simplify your planning and instruction — you want just the fundamental work that produces student growth.
You push in one to two areas per year and maintain the rest. I describe this thinking in the book's conclusion. It's really important.

This actually isn't as time-consuming as it sounds because I'm going to use the same exact intervention for every child, and all but one intervention will be administered with the entire class simultaneously.
First, taking the time to write this out has given me a boost of motivation. It's bolstered my beliefs in the final weeks of school.
Third, I want leaders and teachers to get a sense for how new isn't better by default. I do need to bring some nuance to what I just said, but I've not the time today so I'll end by saying this.
